# wenchang: full documentation

> Persistent, self-organizing memory for AI agents. This file concatenates the pages of https://msiebert.github.io/wenchang/ (Overview, Quickstart, Concepts, Integrate, New MCP server, Existing MCP server, Without MCP, Identity, Storage, Prompts, Reference, Walkthroughs, Status) as Markdown. Page boundaries are marked with `<!-- page: NAME -->`.


<!-- page: index.md -->

# wenchang

> A memory store that AI agents write to on their own judgment. Python library, files in Google Cloud Storage, served to the agent as tools.

wenchang is a Python library that lets an AI agent keep what it learns. During a conversation the agent decides what is worth remembering and saves it as markdown files. In later conversations it reads them back. The files live in Google Cloud Storage.

Install (not on PyPI):

```
pip install "wenchang[mcp] @ git+https://github.com/msiebert/wenchang"
```

The install is one line, but the library does nothing until you configure storage, identity, and prompts. [Quickstart](quickstart.md) covers that.

## Memory the agent decides to keep

Most agents forget everything when a conversation ends. wenchang gives the agent a small set of tools for writing and reading memory. Nothing outside the agent decides what gets saved. The agent notices a character detail, a plot decision, or a style preference, and writes it down.

Say an author is writing a novel with an assistant built on wenchang. The author mentions that the protagonist, Lin Qiao, has grey eyes and grew up in a river town. The agent saves it in a file called `project/p-ninth-examination/characters/lin-qiao.md`:

```
description: Lin Qiao, the protagonist
aliases: Qiao
---
- [stated] Has grey eyes.
- [stated] Grew up in Yunmen, a river town.
```

Weeks later, in a new conversation, the author asks for a scene with Lin Qiao. The agent reads its index, opens that file, and gives her grey eyes. If the author changes their mind, the agent edits that one line.

wenchang does not decide what is worth keeping. A prompt that ships with the library tells the agent how to decide, and you can change that prompt. See [Customizing the prompts](prompts.md).

## How it works

### The agent starts from an index

At the start of each session the agent calls `get_memory_index()`. It gets one entry for every file it has written: scope, area, name, version, a one-line description, and aliases. It does not get file contents. It reads the descriptions, decides which files matter for the current conversation, and opens only those.

```json
// get_memory_index()
{
  "entries": [
    {
      "scope": "project", "area": "characters", "name": "lin-qiao",
      "version": "3",
      "description": "Lin Qiao, the protagonist",
      "aliases": ["Qiao"]
    },
    {
      "scope": "project", "area": "timeline", "name": "main-timeline",
      "version": "1",
      "description": "Order of events in the novel",
      "aliases": ["chronology", "timeline"]
    }
  ],
  "capped": []
}
```
Real entries also carry `sources`, and `last_updated`. If the index gets too big, it is cut at a size limit and the agent lists the rest with `list_prefix`. There is no search over file contents. Descriptions and aliases are how the agent finds things, so the agent keeps them up to date as it writes.

### The agent organizes its own files

The agent has seven tools: `get_memory_index`, `read_file`, `list_prefix`, `write_file`, `append_line`, `replace_fact`, and `delete_file`. Each fact is one line. The agent can add a line, change a line, or drop one. It can rewrite a file, create one, or delete one. It can change a file's description and aliases whenever it writes.

The library sets no schema. The agent decides how to split memory into files, which file a fact belongs in, and what to delete when a fact stops being true. The shipped prompt pushes it toward one file per subject, toward appending to an existing file instead of creating a duplicate, and toward removing a fact completely when the user asks it to forget.

### Scopes and areas

Every file path has this shape:

```
{scope}/{entity_id}/{area}/{name}.md
project/p-ninth-examination/characters/lin-qiao.md
```

A **scope** says who can see a file. You define the scopes. A common set is `user` (private to one person), `project` (shared by a team), and `organization` (shared by everyone, writable only by admins). For a novel, `user` is the author's own preferences, `project` is the manuscript, and `organization` is the publisher. The **entity ID** says whose copy of that scope it is: `u-tianlong` is one author, `p-ninth-examination` is one manuscript.

An **area** is a kind of information inside a scope, such as `characters`, `plot`, `timeline`, or `style` in a manuscript. You can seed the areas you care about in the prompt, for example "project: characters, plot, timeline, style". Or you can tell the agent to choose its own. Either way it can add areas by writing a file in a new one.

Every scope also has a `system/` area. You fill it with curated content. The agent can read it and can never change it.

- **Versioned writes.** Every write names the file version the agent read. If someone else changed the file in the meantime, the write fails and returns the current content, and the agent merges and retries.
- **Plain files.** Each memory is a markdown file in one GCS bucket. The description and aliases are stored as object metadata beside it. You can browse the bucket with ordinary tools.
- **Sensitive data.** The prompt tells the agent never to store financial account numbers, health diagnoses, or anything that suggests the user is a minor. This is prompt guidance. No tool filters content.
## How you use it

wenchang is a library. You put its tools in front of your agent in one of three ways, all sharing the same store, identity rules, and prompt. [Choose an integration path](integrate.md) compares them.

- **A new MCP server.** A short script builds a server with `build_server` and runs it over stdio or HTTP, for Claude Code or any MCP client. [New MCP server](integrate-new-server.md)
- **An existing MCP server.** `register_memory_tools` adds the tools and prompt resource to an mcp 2.x `MCPServer` you already run. [Existing MCP server](integrate-existing-server.md)
- **Without MCP.** `bind_tools` returns the tools as Python methods for your own framework, with JSON Schemas from `tool_schemas`. [Without MCP](integrate-without-mcp.md)

The quickest start is a stdio server in Claude Code:

1. **Install it** and create a GCS bucket for memory files. [Quickstart](quickstart.md#install)
2. **Write the server script.** It picks the storage, says who the caller is, and builds the MCP server:

    ```python
    server = build_server(
        slots=slots,  # your prompt text
        client=InProcessClient(MemoryStore(GcsStorage(bucket))),
        resolver=resolver,  # who is calling, and with which scopes
        policy=policy,  # which roles may write which scopes
        credentials_from_context=credentials_from_context,
        source="inkwell-web",
    )
    server.run("stdio")
    ```

    [Quickstart](quickstart.md#server)
3. **Register it with your MCP client.** For Claude Code, `claude mcp add memory -- python server.py`. [Quickstart](quickstart.md#client)
4. **Tune the prompts.** Four text slots tell the agent what your product is, which scopes exist, and which areas to start with. [Customizing the prompts](prompts.md)
5. **Plug in your own auth** when more than one person uses the server. [Identity and multi-tenant auth](identity.md)
## What wenchang is and is not

wenchang provides the primitives for agent memory. It is not a hosted service and not a complete product.

**wenchang provides:**

- The seven tools the agent calls.
- The memory prompt that teaches the agent how to use them.
- The layer that writes to long-term storage (GCS), with versioned writes and size limits.
- Enforcement of your scope rules: the `system/` area is read-only, and restricted scopes accept only the roles you name.
- An MCP adapter, so the tools work in any MCP client, and JSON Schemas for other tool frameworks.

**You provide:**

- Authentication: verifying who is calling.
- Authorization: mapping each caller to the scopes, entity IDs, and roles they get. wenchang calls your resolver on every tool call and trusts its answer.
- A GCS bucket and credentials.
- The server process: where it runs and how clients reach it.
- Any content filtering beyond what the prompt asks for.

**Not included:**

- Search over file contents.
- A command line tool or ready-made server.
- A remote transport. The tools talk to storage in the same process.
- Storage other than GCS, apart from an in-memory fake for tests.

Version 0.1.0, MIT license, Python 3.11 or newer. See [Status and compatibility](status.md#limitations) for known limits.

---

<!-- page: quickstart.md -->

# Quickstart

This page takes you from nothing to a stdio MCP server that stores memory in GCS and works in Claude Code. The setup is for one developer or a small team that trusts each other. For a server with real users, finish here and then read [Identity and multi-tenant auth](identity.md). To add memory to a server or tool framework you already run, see [Choose an integration path](integrate.md).

wenchang is a library. It has no command line tool, no ready-made server, and no configuration file. You write a short `server.py`.

## What you need

- Python 3.11 or newer.
- A GCP project and a GCS bucket for memory files.
- An MCP client that can launch a stdio server, such as Claude Code.

## 1. Install

wenchang is not on PyPI. Install it from git into the environment the server will run in. The `mcp` extra adds the MCP adapter (`mcp>=2.2,<3`).

```
pip install "wenchang[mcp] @ git+https://github.com/msiebert/wenchang"
```

With uv: `uv add "wenchang[mcp] @ git+https://github.com/msiebert/wenchang"`.

Without MCP, the base package is enough: `pip install "wenchang @ git+https://github.com/msiebert/wenchang"`. See [Integrate without MCP](integrate-without-mcp.md).

> **Compatibility: mcp 2.x `MCPServer` only.** The `mcp` extra installs `mcp>=2.2,<3`, and the adapter targets `mcp.server.mcpserver.MCPServer`. FastMCP servers and mcp 1.x servers do not work: with mcp 1.x installed, importing `wenchang.mcp` raises `ImportError`, and `register_memory_tools` raises `TypeError("server must be an MCPServer, not ...")` for any other server type. For another framework, see [Integrate without MCP](integrate-without-mcp.md).

## 2. Create the bucket

Memory files are objects in one bucket. Create it and give your credentials access:

```
gcloud storage buckets create gs://hanlin-inkwell-memory --project my-gcp-project --location us-central1 --uniform-bucket-level-access
gcloud auth application-default login
gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding gs://hanlin-inkwell-memory --member user:tianlong@example.com --role roles/storage.objectUser
```

wenchang finds credentials through Application Default Credentials, and the server's identity needs `roles/storage.objectUser` on the bucket. [Storage and operations](storage.md#bucket) covers the permissions, the one-bucket access model, and soft delete.

## 3. Write the server

This `server.py` uses GCS storage, three scopes (the author, the manuscript, the publisher), and settings from environment variables.

```python
import os

from google.cloud import storage
from mcp.server.mcpserver import Context

from wenchang.core import MemoryStore
from wenchang.identity import Identity, SandboxResolver, ScopeGrant
from wenchang.mcp import build_server
from wenchang.prompts import PromptSlots
from wenchang.scope import ScopePolicy
from wenchang.storage.gcs import GcsStorage
from wenchang.transport import InProcessClient

slots = PromptSlots(
    purpose=(
        "You have persistent memory of your work helping an author write a novel: reference it "
        "and save to it with these tools whenever you work on a manuscript."
    ),
    scope_guidance=(
        "There are three scopes. `user` is private to the author you are talking with. "
        "`project` is the manuscript, shared by everyone working on it; any of them may write it. "
        "`organization` is Hanlin Press, shared by every author and editor there; only "
        "editors-in-chief may write it. Writes to `user` and `project` need no ask. If a new fact "
        "contradicts one stored in a shared scope, show the stored fact and ask which to keep."
    ),
    seed_areas=(
        "- user: preferences, workflows\n"
        "- project: characters, plot, timeline, style\n"
        "- organization: conventions\n\n"
        "Every scope also has a `system/` area."
    ),
)

# Each person sets their own WENCHANG_USER. Everyone on a manuscript shares WENCHANG_PROJECT.
identity = Identity(
    grants={
        "user": ScopeGrant(os.environ["WENCHANG_USER"], "owner"),
        "project": ScopeGrant(os.environ["WENCHANG_PROJECT"], "member"),
        "organization": ScopeGrant(os.environ["WENCHANG_ORG"], "member"),
    }
)

# Application Default Credentials; the bucket must already exist.
bucket = storage.Client(project="my-gcp-project").bucket(os.environ["WENCHANG_BUCKET"])
store = MemoryStore(GcsStorage(bucket), scope_priority=("user", "project", "organization"))


def credentials_from_context(ctx: Context) -> None:
    return None  # SandboxResolver ignores credentials.


server = build_server(
    slots=slots,
    client=InProcessClient(store),
    resolver=SandboxResolver(identity),
    # Only editors-in-chief (admins) write organization.
    policy=ScopePolicy({"organization": frozenset({"admin", "owner"})}),
    credentials_from_context=credentials_from_context,
    source="claude-code",
    product="Inkwell",
)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    server.run("stdio")
```

What each part does:

- **`PromptSlots`** is the text that tells the agent about your deployment. See [Customizing the prompts](prompts.md).
- **`Identity`** says who the caller is: one `ScopeGrant(entity_id, role)` per scope. The entity ID becomes the second path segment, so this user's private files live under `user/<their id>/`. Here the identity comes from the environment and is trusted. [Identity and multi-tenant auth](identity.md) replaces this with a resolver that verifies each request.
- **`MemoryStore`** applies the rules (size limits, versioned writes, index order) on top of a `Storage`. `GcsStorage` is the storage that talks to your bucket. `scope_priority` decides which scopes the size-capped startup index keeps first.
- **`InProcessClient`** connects the tools to the store in the same process.
- **`ScopePolicy`** lists the roles that may write a scope. Here only `admin` and `owner` may write `organization`, and the identity above is a plain `member`, so the agent can read the press's files and cannot change them. Scopes not listed are open to anyone with a grant. Writes to `system/` are always refused.
- **`source`** is recorded in each file's `sources` metadata, so you can tell which app wrote what. **`product`** puts your product's name in each tool description.

Check that it builds, without starting it:

```
WENCHANG_USER=u-tianlong WENCHANG_PROJECT=p-ninth-examination WENCHANG_ORG=o-hanlin-press WENCHANG_BUCKET=hanlin-inkwell-memory python -c "import server; print(server.server)"
```

## 4. Register it with your client

A stdio MCP client starts the server as a child process. Give it the interpreter that has wenchang installed, an absolute path to the script, and the environment the script reads.

For Claude Code, put this in the project's `.mcp.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "memory": {
      "command": "/path/to/venv/bin/python",
      "args": ["/path/to/server.py"],
      "env": {
        "WENCHANG_BUCKET": "hanlin-inkwell-memory",
        "WENCHANG_ORG": "o-hanlin-press",
        "WENCHANG_PROJECT": "p-ninth-examination",
        "WENCHANG_USER": "u-tianlong"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

`WENCHANG_USER` differs per person, so in a shared repo keep that one out of `.mcp.json` and set it per person. The same registration from the command line, for just you:

```
claude mcp add memory -e WENCHANG_BUCKET=hanlin-inkwell-memory -e WENCHANG_ORG=o-hanlin-press -e WENCHANG_PROJECT=p-ninth-examination -e WENCHANG_USER=u-tianlong -- /path/to/venv/bin/python /path/to/server.py
```

The server sends the memory prompt as its `instructions`, and also serves it as the resource `wenchang://memory-prompt` for clients that ignore `instructions`. In Claude Code the tools show up as `mcp__memory__get_memory_index`, `mcp__memory__read_file`, and so on. `/mcp` shows whether the server connected.

## 5. Try it

Tell the agent something worth keeping:

> Lin Qiao has grey eyes and grew up in Yunmen, a river town.

It should call `get_memory_index`, then write a file. Start a new session and ask for a scene with Lin Qiao. It should read the index, open the file, and use what it saved. Look at what was stored:

```
gcloud storage ls --recursive gs://hanlin-inkwell-memory/project/p-ninth-examination/
```

Each object is a markdown file. The description and aliases are in the object's custom metadata. If nothing is written, check that the agent listed the memory tools and read the server's `instructions`. Memory is only as good as the prompt, so also read [Customizing the prompts](prompts.md).

## Seed curated content

The `system/` area holds content that people maintain. Here that is Hanlin Press's house style. The agent can read it but cannot write it. You write it with a script that uses the store directly, which has no `system/` restriction.

```python
import os
from datetime import UTC, datetime

from google.cloud import storage

from wenchang.core import MemoryStore
from wenchang.file_format import FileMetadata
from wenchang.paths import build_path
from wenchang.storage.gcs import GcsStorage
from wenchang.transport import InProcessClient

bucket = storage.Client(project="my-gcp-project").bucket(os.environ["WENCHANG_BUCKET"])
client = InProcessClient(MemoryStore(GcsStorage(bucket)))

# Goes through the store directly, so it may write system/.
path = build_path("organization", "o-hanlin-press", "system", "house-style")
client.write_file(
    path,
    "- [system] Dialogue uses double quotation marks.\n"
    "- [system] Spelling follows British English.\n",
    FileMetadata(
        description="Hanlin Press house style",
        aliases=("style guide", "house style"),
        sources=frozenset(),
        last_updated=datetime.now(UTC),
    ),
    None,  # create; pass the current version to replace
    source="seed-job",
)
```

Seeded files appear in the agent's index like any others, and the `system/` entries come first.

## Run it without GCS

For development, `InMemoryStorage()` from `wenchang.storage.memory` replaces `GcsStorage(bucket)`. Everything is lost when the process exits, and a stdio server starts a fresh process for every client session, so it forgets between sessions.

To test against the real GCS API locally, run the emulator the repository's integration tests use:

```
docker run -d --rm --name wenchang-fake-gcs -p 4443:4443 fsouza/fake-gcs-server -scheme http -port 4443
```

Then point the client at it:

```python
from google.auth.credentials import AnonymousCredentials
from google.cloud import storage

client = storage.Client(
    project="test",
    credentials=AnonymousCredentials(),
    client_options={"api_endpoint": "http://localhost:4443"},
)
bucket = client.bucket("wenchang-dev")
if not bucket.exists():
    bucket = client.create_bucket("wenchang-dev")
```

- [Customizing the prompts](prompts.md): tell the agent about your scopes and areas.
- [Identity and multi-tenant auth](identity.md): serve many users over HTTP.
- [Integrate: a new MCP server](integrate-new-server.md): every `build_server` argument, and stdio or HTTP.
- [Storage and operations](storage.md): costs, limits, and erasing a user's memory.

<!-- page: concepts.md -->

# Concepts

How wenchang addresses and versions memory files, and the limits it enforces. These hold on every integration path. For the tools themselves see the [reference](reference.md); for how files are stored in GCS see [Storage and operations](storage.md).

## Path shape

Every memory file is stored at

```
{scope}/{entity_id}/{area}/{name}.md
```

For example `project/p-ninth-examination/characters/lin-qiao.md`. Agents never write the path. The tools take `(scope, area, name)` and the tool layer fills in `entity_id` from the caller's identity grant for that scope, so a caller can only reach its own entities. Results name a file by its `scope`, `area`, and `name`; they never include the storage path.

An **entity** is everything under one `{scope}/{entity_id}/` prefix: one user's private memory, or one project's shared memory.

## Scopes

A scope is an adopter-defined visibility tier. The library defines no scope names; a typical set is `user` (private), `project` (shared), and `organization` (shared, writes need an admin or owner role). A scope must be one of the scopes the session's identity has a grant for; otherwise the call fails with an `InvalidArgumentError` listing the available scopes. See [Identity and multi-tenant auth](identity.md) for how grants are made.

## Areas

An area groups files within a scope. The tool layer requires an area to be a lowercase slug matching `^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]*$`. Areas are created implicitly by writing a file in them. The prompt's `seed_areas` slot suggests starting areas; the agent may create more.

## Names

A name is the file's stem, passed without `.md`. It must be a valid path segment: non-empty, not `.` or `..`, with no `/`, backslash, or control character, and the tool layer additionally rejects invisible, separator, and noncharacter code points. Names must be valid UTF-8.

## The system/ area

Every scope has an area named exactly `system`. It holds curated content that people maintain and replace wholesale. The agent can read it (any area may be read) but every mutating tool refuses it with `RestrictedScopeError` (reason `system_read_only`). Seeding jobs and admin tooling write it through the core `MemoryStore`, which applies no restrictions; see [Seed curated content](quickstart.md#seed). In the startup index, `system/` entries come first across all scopes.

## Fact lines

A memory file body is made of fact lines, one per line:

```
- [stated] Has grey eyes.
```

The pattern is `- [<label>] <text>` with a non-empty text. The label records how the fact is known:

| Label | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `stated` | The user told the agent directly. |
| `observed` | The agent saw it in a tool result, session data, or behavior. |
| `inferred` | The agent concluded it from a pattern across several observations. |
| `system` | Curated content. The prompt tells the agent never to write a new `[system]` line. |

`append_line` accepts only a single well-formed fact line. Other lines in a body are tolerated and preserved verbatim. An end date, if the user states one, is written into the fact's text as prose; there are no per-fact timestamps.

## File metadata

Each file carries four metadata fields, stored beside the body as custom metadata on the stored object, not inside the markdown. Tool results and the index show them under these names; [Storage and operations](storage.md#metadata) gives the stored keys and encodings.

| Field | Type | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `description` | string, one line | What the file is about. Part of the agent's search surface. `write_file` replaces it; `append_line` and `replace_fact` replace it only if one is passed. |
| `aliases` | list of strings, ordered | Other names the subject is looked up by. `write_file` replaces the whole set; `append_line` and `replace_fact` add new aliases, keeping existing ones and their order. |
| `sources` | set of strings | Surface names (the `source` you configure) that have written the file. Only ever grows; returned sorted. |
| `last_updated` | UTC timestamp | Set by the store's clock on every write; rendered as ISO 8601 with a `Z` suffix. |

There is no content search. `description` and `aliases` are the entire search surface; the agent reads the index and matches on them.

## Optimistic concurrency

Every file has an opaque `version` (the GCS generation under `GcsStorage`). Every mutating tool takes `expected_version`, the version the agent read; the write succeeds only if the file is still at that version. `write_file` with `expected_version=null` creates the file and fails if it already exists. A mismatch returns a recoverable `VersionConflictError` carrying the current content and version.

`replace_fact` re-reads and retries up to three times when a concurrent write races it, re-checking the match each time; if the file's version moved but `old_string` still matches exactly once, it applies against the current content. `append_line` has no automatic re-apply: a stale version is a conflict. Versions are opaque: never parse, compare, or order them.

## Limits

| Limit | Default | Where set |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Per-file content size | 16384 bytes (UTF-8) | `MemoryStore(max_file_bytes=...)` |
| Startup index size | 65536 bytes; see [Index cost](storage.md#index-cost) for how entries are sized | `MemoryStore(index_max_bytes=...)` |
| `list_prefix` page size | 100 entries | `MemoryStore(list_page_size=...)` |
| Files per entity | 500 files, `system/` not counted; see [Files per entity](storage.md#file-cap) | `MemoryStore(max_files_per_entity=...)` |
| `replace_fact` attempts | 3 | fixed |

When the index overflows its budget, the remaining files are reported under `capped` by area, with the count omitted, and the agent pages them with `list_prefix`. Index order: `system/` areas of all scopes first; then scopes in `scope_priority` order (unlisted scopes last, as one tier); within each tier, most recently updated first.

<!-- page: integrate.md -->

# Choose an integration path

The memory tools are plain Python methods. There are three ways to put them in front of an agent. All three share the same store, identity resolver, scope policy, and prompt; they differ only in who registers the tools and how a call reaches them.

| Path | Use it when | Entry point |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [A new MCP server](integrate-new-server.md) | You want a standalone memory server for an MCP client such as Claude Code, over stdio or HTTP. | `wenchang.mcp.build_server` |
| [An existing MCP server](integrate-existing-server.md) | You already run an mcp 2.x `MCPServer` with your own tools, auth, and middleware, and want memory on it. | `wenchang.mcp.register_memory_tools` |
| [Without MCP](integrate-without-mcp.md) | Your agent uses another tool framework, or calls a model API directly with its own tool loop. | `wenchang.tools.bind_tools` |

The MCP paths need the `mcp` extra and work only with mcp 2.x `MCPServer`. The path without MCP needs only the base package.

Whichever path you take:

- [Concepts](concepts.md) explains paths, scopes, files, versions, and limits.
- [Identity and multi-tenant auth](identity.md) explains how a caller becomes a set of scopes.
- [Customizing the prompts](prompts.md) explains the prompt the agent needs alongside the tools.
- [Storage and operations](storage.md) covers the bucket, costs, caching, and erasure.

---

HTML version: <https://msiebert.github.io/wenchang/integrate.html>


<!-- page: integrate-new-server.md -->

# Integrate: a new MCP server

`wenchang.mcp.build_server(...)` returns a new mcp 2.x `MCPServer` that carries the memory prompt as its `instructions`, the seven memory tools, and the prompt resource `wenchang://memory-prompt`. You run it with `server.run(...)`. [Quickstart](quickstart.md) builds one end to end for Claude Code; this page covers every argument and both transports.

> **Compatibility: mcp 2.x `MCPServer` only.** The `mcp` extra installs `mcp>=2.2,<3`, and the adapter targets `mcp.server.mcpserver.MCPServer`. FastMCP servers and mcp 1.x servers do not work: with mcp 1.x installed, importing `wenchang.mcp` raises `ImportError`, and `register_memory_tools` raises `TypeError("server must be an MCPServer, not ...")` for any other server type. For another framework, see [Integrate without MCP](integrate-without-mcp.md).

Install with the extra: `pip install "wenchang[mcp] @ git+https://github.com/msiebert/wenchang"`.

## Arguments

Every argument is keyword-only. `build_server` checks them all before it creates the server, and raises `TypeError` or `ValueError` for a bad one.

| Argument | Required | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `slots` | yes | A `PromptSlots`. The server's `instructions` are `build_memory_prompt(slots)`. See [Customizing the prompts](prompts.md). |
| `client` | yes | A `TransportClient`, normally `InProcessClient(MemoryStore(...))`. Tool calls run concurrently on worker threads, so it must be thread-safe. |
| `resolver` | yes | Your `IdentityResolver`. It runs on every tool call. See [Identity](identity.md). |
| `policy` | yes | A `ScopePolicy`: the roles that may write each scope. |
| `credentials_from_context` | yes | A plain (non-async) function that takes the MCP request `Context` and returns the raw credentials your resolver verifies. See [Credentials](#credentials). |
| `source` | yes | The surface name added to each written file's `sources` metadata. Non-empty. |
| `product` | no | Your product's name, put in the first line of each tool description. One non-empty line. |
| `tool_prefix` | no | Registers each tool as `{tool_prefix}_{name}`. 1 to 64 letters, digits, `_` or `-`, starting and ending with a letter or digit. |
| `on_call` | no | A plain function called with a `ToolCallRecord` after every tool call. See [Observing calls](#on-call). |
| `name` | no | The server name. Default `"wenchang"`. |

The server's version is the installed wenchang version. [Names on the tools](prompts.md#naming) has more on `product`, `tool_prefix`, and `source`.

## Credentials

Every tool call runs `credentials_from_context(ctx)`, passes the result to your resolver, and binds that caller's own tools. `ctx.headers` holds the request headers on HTTP and is `None` on stdio. Return the raw value and leave verification to the resolver. If the function raises, the call fails with a permanent `ResolverFailureError`, and only the exception's type is logged, since its message may carry the credential.

## Transports

- **stdio.** `server.run("stdio")`. The client starts one server process per session, so identity usually comes from the process environment: a variable holding a token, or the grants themselves for a single-developer setup as in [Quickstart](quickstart.md#server). Return it from `credentials_from_context` as `os.environ.get("MEMORY_TOKEN")` and let the resolver verify it.
- **Streamable HTTP.** `server.run("streamable-http", host="0.0.0.0", port=8000)` serves the MCP endpoint at `/mcp` (mcp's defaults are host `127.0.0.1` and port 8000). Put TLS in front of it. Each request carries its own credentials in headers, so one process serves many callers. The MCP SDK also has its own auth options on `MCPServer` (`auth`, `token_verifier`) if you want requests rejected before they reach wenchang; see the `mcp` documentation. [Identity](identity.md#example) has a complete multi-tenant HTTP server, which has been run against fake-gcs-server and driven by mcp's streamable-HTTP client.

## Observing calls

`on_call` receives a `wenchang.observer.ToolCallRecord` after every tool call (`wenchang.mcp` re-exports it). On this path:

- `tool` is the registered name, prefix included.
- `request_id` is the MCP request's ID, for correlating records that arrive in completion order.
- `duration_s` covers reading credentials, binding, the tool, and rendering.
- It runs on worker threads, so it must be thread-safe and fast.

Calls MCP rejects while validating arguments never produce a record. An exception the observer raises is logged at ERROR and swallowed. The [reference](reference.md#telemetry) lists every field.

## Next

- [Identity and multi-tenant auth](identity.md): a resolver for real users.
- [Integrate: an existing mcp 2.x server](integrate-existing-server.md): the same tools on a server you already run.

---

HTML version: <https://msiebert.github.io/wenchang/integrate-new-server.html>


<!-- page: integrate-existing-server.md -->

# Integrate: an existing mcp 2.x server

`build_server` creates a new server. To add memory to an `MCPServer` you already run, with your own tools, auth, and middleware, call `wenchang.mcp.register_memory_tools(server, ...)`. It adds the seven memory tools and the `wenchang://memory-prompt` resource to that server.

> **Compatibility: mcp 2.x `MCPServer` only.** The `mcp` extra installs `mcp>=2.2,<3`, and the adapter targets `mcp.server.mcpserver.MCPServer`. FastMCP servers and mcp 1.x servers do not work: with mcp 1.x installed, importing `wenchang.mcp` raises `ImportError`, and `register_memory_tools` raises `TypeError("server must be an MCPServer, not ...")` for any other server type, before it registers anything. For another framework, see [Integrate without MCP](integrate-without-mcp.md).

Install with the extra: `pip install "wenchang[mcp] @ git+https://github.com/msiebert/wenchang"`.

## Register the tools

`register_memory_tools` takes the server, then keyword arguments: `prompt`, `client`, `resolver`, `policy`, `credentials_from_context`, `source`, and optionally `product`, `tool_prefix`, and `on_call`. They mean the same as for [`build_server`](integrate-new-server.md#arguments), except that you pass the prompt text instead of the slots.

```python
import logging

from mcp.server.mcpserver import Context, MCPServer

from wenchang.core import MemoryStore
from wenchang.identity import Identity, SandboxResolver, ScopeGrant
from wenchang.mcp import ToolCallRecord, memory_instructions, register_memory_tools
from wenchang.prompts import PromptSlots
from wenchang.scope import ScopePolicy
from wenchang.storage.memory import InMemoryStorage
from wenchang.transport import InProcessClient

log = logging.getLogger("inkwell.calls")

slots = PromptSlots(
    purpose="You have persistent memory of your work helping an author write a novel.",
    scope_guidance=(
        "There is one scope, user, and it is private to the author you are talking with."
    ),
    seed_areas="- user: preferences, workflows, research\n\nEvery scope also has a `system/` area.",
)
identity = Identity(grants={"user": ScopeGrant("u-tianlong", "owner")})


def credentials_from_context(ctx: Context) -> str | None:
    # Over HTTP, return the raw credential and let your resolver verify it.
    # ctx.headers is None on stdio.
    return (ctx.headers or {}).get("authorization")


def on_call(record: ToolCallRecord) -> None:
    # Runs on worker threads after every call; keep it fast and thread-safe.
    log.info("%s error=%s %.3fs", record.tool, record.is_error, record.duration_s)


prompt = memory_instructions(slots)

# Your existing server, with your own tools and middleware.
server = MCPServer("hanlin-tools", instructions=prompt)

register_memory_tools(
    server,
    prompt=prompt,
    client=InProcessClient(MemoryStore(InMemoryStorage())),
    resolver=SandboxResolver(identity),
    policy=ScopePolicy({}),
    credentials_from_context=credentials_from_context,
    source="hanlin-tools",
    product="Inkwell",
    tool_prefix="inkwell",  # tools are registered as inkwell_read_file, inkwell_write_file, ...
    on_call=on_call,
)
```

## The prompt

The agent needs the memory prompt as well as the tools. `memory_instructions(slots)` returns it. Pass the same text as the server's `instructions` and as `prompt`; `prompt` is what the `wenchang://memory-prompt` resource serves, for clients that ignore `instructions`. If your server already has instructions, include the memory prompt in them; [Customizing the prompts](prompts.md#fixed) shows how to append sections of your own.

After registering, `register_memory_tools` checks the server's `instructions`. If they do not contain `prompt`, it logs a warning on the `wenchang.mcp` logger and registers anyway.

## Name collisions

`MCPServer` only logs a duplicate tool or resource, so `register_memory_tools` checks first. If any memory tool name or the resource URI is already registered on the server, it raises `ValueError("cannot register memory tools: already registered on the server: ...")`, naming each collision, and registers nothing. Set `tool_prefix` to register the tools as `{tool_prefix}_read_file` and so on. The resource URI has no prefix, so a server holds one memory prompt resource.

Any invalid argument also raises before anything is registered.

## Credentials and observing calls

Each tool call reads credentials with your `credentials_from_context`, resolves them, and binds that caller's tools, exactly as on a [new server](integrate-new-server.md#credentials). Your own auth middleware can reject a request before it reaches wenchang; whatever reaches `credentials_from_context` still goes through your resolver. Tool calls run concurrently on worker threads, so `client` must be thread-safe.

`on_call` behaves as on a new server: `tool` is the registered name, prefix included, `request_id` is the MCP request's ID, and the observer runs on worker threads. See [Observing calls](integrate-new-server.md#on-call) and the [field reference](reference.md#telemetry).

## Next

- [Identity and multi-tenant auth](identity.md): the resolver behind `credentials_from_context`.
- [Integrate without MCP](integrate-without-mcp.md): the same tools in another framework.

---

HTML version: <https://msiebert.github.io/wenchang/integrate-existing-server.html>


<!-- page: integrate-without-mcp.md -->

# Integrate without MCP

The memory tools are methods on a Python object. If your agent runs on another tool framework, or on your own loop over a model API, call them directly. Nothing is registered anywhere until you register it.

## Install

The base package is enough. It needs no `mcp`:

```
pip install "wenchang @ git+https://github.com/msiebert/wenchang"
```

With uv: `uv add "wenchang @ git+https://github.com/msiebert/wenchang"`.

## The tools are methods

`wenchang.tools.bind_tools(client, resolver, credentials, policy, *, source, product=None, on_call=None)` resolves the caller's identity and returns a `MemoryTools` for that identity. On it:

- `tools.tools()` maps each of the seven tool names to its bound method, in `wenchang.tools.TOOL_NAMES` order.
- `tools.descriptions()` maps each name to the description to show the model, with `product` named in each first line. Register this text, not the methods' docstrings.

The methods take the same arguments as the tools in the [reference](reference.md#tools) and return result objects. Nothing else is exposed: no prompt, no registration, no transport.

If you have already resolved the identity yourself, `MemoryTools(client, identity, policy, *, source, product=None, on_call=None)` builds the same object from an `Identity`.

## Bind per request

`bind_tools` calls your resolver once and fixes that identity for the object's lifetime. A multi-tenant service binds per request, or per session if a session has one caller, never once per process. Binding runs the resolver and builds a small object.

The store, the client, the resolver, and the policy are built once per process and shared.

If the resolver returns a `ResolutionFailure` or raises, `bind_tools` raises `ResolverFailureError` (permanent). Render it like any tool error. The model then has no memory for that request.

## Tool schemas

`wenchang.schemas.tool_schemas(product=None)` returns a read-only mapping from tool name to `ToolSchema`, one per tool, in `TOOL_NAMES` order. Give these to your framework instead of writing argument models by hand. `error_schema()` returns the schema shared by every `render_error` payload.

| Field | Type | Contents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | string | The bare tool name, such as `read_file`. |
| `description` | string | The tool's description, the same as `tool_descriptions(product)[name]`. |
| `input` | dict | JSON Schema of the tool's arguments, with defaults for optional ones. |
| `output` | dict | JSON Schema of the `render_result` payload on success. |
| `error` | dict | JSON Schema of the `render_error` payload on failure; the same as `error_schema()`. |

Every schema is JSON Schema draft 2020-12 and closed (`additionalProperties: false`). Each call builds fresh dicts, so you can change them without affecting later calls.

Validate the model's arguments against `input` before calling the method, as most frameworks do from the parameter schema. The method is called with `**arguments`, so a missing or unknown argument raises a `TypeError` that `render_error` reports as an opaque `internal` error. Here `ToolDef` stands in for your framework's tool definition, for one session's tools:

```python
from collections.abc import Callable
from dataclasses import dataclass

from wenchang.core import MemoryStore
from wenchang.identity import Identity, SandboxResolver, ScopeGrant
from wenchang.schemas import tool_schemas
from wenchang.scope import ScopePolicy
from wenchang.storage.memory import InMemoryStorage
from wenchang.tools import MemoryTools, bind_tools, render_error, render_result
from wenchang.transport import InProcessClient


@dataclass
class ToolDef:  # stand-in for your framework's tool definition
    name: str
    description: str
    parameters: dict[str, object]
    handler: Callable[[dict[str, object]], dict[str, object]]


def handler(tools: MemoryTools, name: str) -> Callable[[dict[str, object]], dict[str, object]]:
    method = tools.tools()[name]

    def call(arguments: dict[str, object]) -> dict[str, object]:
        # The framework has already validated `arguments` against `s.input`.
        try:
            return render_result(method(**arguments))  # matches the schema's output
        except Exception as exc:
            return render_error(exc)  # matches the schema's error

    return call


client = InProcessClient(MemoryStore(InMemoryStorage()))
resolver = SandboxResolver(Identity(grants={"user": ScopeGrant("u-tianlong", "owner")}))
tools = bind_tools(client, resolver, None, ScopePolicy({}), source="inkwell-cli", product="Inkwell")

defs: dict[str, ToolDef] = {}
for s in tool_schemas(product="Inkwell").values():
    call = handler(tools, s.name)
    defs[s.name] = ToolDef(name=s.name, description=s.description, parameters=s.input, handler=call)

# A NotFoundError payload, valid against tool_schemas()["read_file"].error.
print(defs["read_file"].handler({"scope": "user", "area": "notes", "name": "tea"}))
```

The schemas assume on-contract output and standard tool-use modes:

- **Every field is required.** An on-contract `TransportClient` always produces every field, so each output field is marked required. `render_result` drops a field whose value has the wrong type, which an off-contract client can produce; strict validation rejects that payload.
- **Errors are wenchang's own.** The error schema covers the error classes wenchang raises. A `WenchangError` subclass of your own validates only if it reuses these attribute names, types, and `reason` values.
- **Input schemas target standard tool use.** They work as-is with Anthropic tool use and OpenAI function calling. OpenAI's strict mode requires every property in `required`, so optional arguments must become required and nullable; Gemini function declarations reject `anyOf`, `additionalProperties`, and `default`. A host using either must transform `input` first.

## Results and errors

Tool methods return result objects and raise exceptions. `wenchang.tools.render_result(value)` turns a return value into the JSON-safe dict to show the model, and `render_error(exc)` turns any exception into the error payload, with the category and repair details described under [errors](reference.md#errors). These are the same payloads the MCP adapter sends. An unexpected exception renders as an `internal` error with a generic message, so internals never reach the model.

## A complete example

This binds per request with an in-memory store, dispatches each call by name with arguments checked against the schema, and renders a result and an error. The asserts show what comes back.

```python
from wenchang.core import MemoryStore
from wenchang.errors import InvalidArgumentError
from wenchang.identity import Identity, ResolutionFailure, ScopeGrant
from wenchang.observer import ToolCallRecord
from wenchang.schemas import tool_schemas
from wenchang.scope import ScopePolicy
from wenchang.storage.memory import InMemoryStorage
from wenchang.tools import bind_tools, render_error, render_result
from wenchang.transport import InProcessClient

USERS = {"tok-tianlong": "u-tianlong", "tok-diya": "u-diya"}  # stand-in for your IdP


class TokenResolver:
    """Maps a bearer token to the caller's grants. Must not raise."""

    def resolve(self, credentials: str | None) -> Identity | ResolutionFailure:
        user_id = USERS.get(credentials or "")
        if user_id is None:
            return ResolutionFailure("Invalid or expired token.")
        return Identity(grants={"user": ScopeGrant(user_id, "owner")})


# Built once per process and shared by every request; both must be thread-safe.
client = InProcessClient(MemoryStore(InMemoryStorage()))
resolver = TokenResolver()
policy = ScopePolicy({})
schemas = tool_schemas(product="Inkwell")
records: list[ToolCallRecord] = []

# Register these with your framework once: name, description, and parameter schema.
definitions = [
    {"name": s.name, "description": s.description, "input_schema": s.input}
    for s in schemas.values()
]


def check_arguments(name: str, arguments: dict[str, object]) -> None:
    # Your framework normally validates against the input schema; this checks names only.
    schema: dict = schemas[name].input
    for key in arguments:
        if key not in schema["properties"]:
            raise InvalidArgumentError(key, "not a parameter of this tool")
    for key in schema.get("required", []):
        if key not in arguments:
            raise InvalidArgumentError(key, "required")


def run_tool_calls(
    token: str | None, calls: list[tuple[str, dict[str, object]]]
) -> list[dict[str, object]]:
    """Run one request's tool calls as the caller the token names."""
    try:
        # Resolve once per request, never once per process.
        tools = bind_tools(
            client,
            resolver,
            token,
            policy,
            source="inkwell-api",
            product="Inkwell",
            on_call=records.append,
        )
    except Exception as exc:  # ResolverFailureError: no memory for this request
        return [render_error(exc) for _ in calls]
    methods = tools.tools()
    payloads: list[dict[str, object]] = []
    for name, arguments in calls:
        try:
            check_arguments(name, arguments)
            payloads.append(render_result(methods[name](**arguments)))
        except Exception as exc:
            payloads.append(render_error(exc))
    return payloads


created, missing = run_tool_calls(
    "tok-tianlong",
    [
        (
            "write_file",
            {
                "scope": "user",
                "area": "preferences",
                "name": "prose-style",
                "content": "- [stated] Writes in close third person, past tense.\n",
                "description": "Prose style preferences",
                "aliases": ["narration", "voice"],
                "expected_version": None,
            },
        ),
        ("read_file", {"scope": "user", "area": "preferences", "name": "tea"}),
    ],
)
assert created["name"] == "prose-style" and created["sources"] == ["inkwell-api"]
assert missing["error"] == "NotFoundError" and missing["category"] == "recoverable"

[denied] = run_tool_calls("tok-expired", [("get_memory_index", {})])
assert denied["error"] == "ResolverFailureError" and denied["category"] == "permanent"

# One record per tool call; request_id is None for direct calls.
assert [(r.tool, r.is_error, r.request_id) for r in records] == [
    ("write_file", False, None),
    ("read_file", True, None),
]
print(created["version"], missing["message"])
```

## Threads and async hosts

Calls are synchronous. Under `GcsStorage` each one blocks on one or more GCS round trips; `get_memory_index` lists every object in the caller's entities unless an [index cache](storage.md#index-cache) serves it. If your host runs tool calls from several threads, the store and client you share must be safe to call from several threads; `InMemoryStorage` is. An async host runs each call in a worker thread, for example `await asyncio.to_thread(method, **arguments)`, so it does not block the event loop.

## Observing calls

`bind_tools(..., on_call=...)` delivers one `ToolCallRecord` per tool call. On this path:

- `tool` is the bare method name, such as `read_file`.
- `arguments` holds every parameter by name, with defaults filled.
- `result` is `render_result` of the return value, or `render_error` of the raised error; `is_error` says which.
- `request_id` is `None`.
- `duration_s` is the wall time of the tool method only.

The observer runs synchronously on the calling thread, before the call returns or raises, so correlate records with a contextvar or thread-local. `bind_tools` checks `on_call` before it runs the resolver. A call Python rejects for its arguments never produces a record. An exception the observer raises is logged at ERROR and swallowed. Records contain memory content, so treat them as sensitive. The [reference](reference.md#telemetry) lists every field.

This observer logs and counts calls without recording arguments or results:

```python
import logging
import threading
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
from contextlib import suppress

from wenchang.core import MemoryStore
from wenchang.errors import NotFoundError
from wenchang.identity import Identity, SandboxResolver, ScopeGrant
from wenchang.observer import ToolCallRecord
from wenchang.scope import ScopePolicy
from wenchang.storage.memory import InMemoryStorage
from wenchang.tools import bind_tools
from wenchang.transport import InProcessClient

log = logging.getLogger("inkwell.memory")

# Stand-ins for your metrics client: a call counter and per-tool latencies.
lock = threading.Lock()
calls: Counter[tuple[str, str]] = Counter()
latencies: defaultdict[str, list[float]] = defaultdict(list)


def on_call(record: ToolCallRecord) -> None:
    # arguments and result carry memory content; log only the call's shape.
    category = record.result.get("category") if record.is_error else None
    log.info(
        "memory tool=%s is_error=%s category=%s duration_s=%.3f",
        record.tool,
        record.is_error,
        category,
        record.duration_s,
    )
    with lock:  # under MCP, observers run on worker threads
        calls[(record.tool, str(category or "ok"))] += 1
        latencies[record.tool].append(record.duration_s)


client = InProcessClient(MemoryStore(InMemoryStorage()))
resolver = SandboxResolver(Identity(grants={"user": ScopeGrant("u-tianlong", "owner")}))
tools = bind_tools(client, resolver, None, ScopePolicy({}), source="inkwell-cli", on_call=on_call)

tools.get_memory_index()  # on_call has run by the time this returns
with suppress(NotFoundError):  # on_call sees it first: is_error=True, category=recoverable
    tools.read_file("user", "preferences", "csv")
print(calls)
```

## What you provide

- **The prompt.** The model needs the memory prompt alongside the tools. Put `build_memory_prompt(slots)` from `wenchang.prompts` in your system prompt; it has `##` headings and no top-level heading. See [Customizing the prompts](prompts.md).
- **Identity.** A resolver and a scope policy. See [Identity and multi-tenant auth](identity.md).
- **Storage.** A `MemoryStore` over `GcsStorage`, or `InMemoryStorage` for tests. See [Storage and operations](storage.md).

---

HTML version: <https://msiebert.github.io/wenchang/integrate-without-mcp.html>


<!-- page: identity.md -->

# Identity and multi-tenant auth

wenchang does not authenticate anyone. You decide who the caller is. wenchang takes your answer and enforces it: the caller can only reach the scopes and entities you grant, and can only write the scopes your policy allows.

In the legend, Wenchang's two attendants are Tianlong, who cannot hear, and Diya, who cannot speak. That way no secret gets out. A resolver is the same arrangement in Python.

## How identity flows

Every tool call goes through the same chain, on every integration path:

```
credentials          raw, untrusted data from the request
   |  credentials_from_context(ctx)    (MCP: runs on every tool call)
   |  or your code passes them         (direct: bind_tools(..., credentials, ...))
   v
resolver.resolve(credentials)          verifies them; returns Identity or ResolutionFailure
   v
Identity                               scope -> ScopeGrant(entity_id, role)
   v
path                                   {scope}/{entity_id}/{area}/{name}.md, from the grant
   v
ScopePolicy                            may this role write this scope?
```

The agent passes only `scope`, `area`, and `name`. The entity ID always comes from the caller's grant, so a caller cannot name another tenant's path. Reads need only a grant; writes also need a role the policy allows.

| Piece | What it owns | In an org, project, and user deployment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Credentials | Whatever the request carries. Never trusted on their own. | A bearer token, plus an `X-Project-Id` header naming the open project. |
| `credentials_from_context` (MCP) or the caller (direct) | Getting credentials out of the request. No verification. | Reads the `Authorization` and `X-Project-Id` headers. |
| `IdentityResolver` | Verifying credentials and deciding the grants. Must not raise. | Verifies the token with your identity provider, then checks project membership in your database. |
| `Identity` | One `ScopeGrant(entity_id, role)` per scope the caller may use. | `user`: the user's ID, role `owner`. `project`: the project's ID, the user's role on it. `organization`: the org's ID, `member` or `admin`. |
| Path | Where a file lives, built from the grant. | `user/u-tianlong/...`, `project/p-ninth-examination/...`, `organization/o-hanlin-press/...`. |
| `ScopePolicy` | Which roles may write each scope. Unlisted scopes are open to any grant. | `organization` writable by `admin` and `owner` only. |

## What you provide

Three pieces plug in.

1. **`credentials_from_context(ctx)`** reads the caller's raw credentials from the MCP request. It must be a plain function, not async. Over HTTP, `ctx.headers` holds the request headers. On stdio it is `None`, so a stdio server reads credentials from its own environment instead. Return the raw value and do not trust it here. Without MCP there is no such function: you pass the credentials to `bind_tools` yourself.
2. **A resolver** with one method, `resolve(credentials) -> Identity | ResolutionFailure`. It verifies the credentials and returns an `Identity`: a mapping from scope name to `ScopeGrant(entity_id, role)`. Roles are your own words (`owner`, `member`, `admin`).
3. **A `ScopePolicy`** mapping a scope to the set of roles allowed to write it. A scope not listed is open to every role that holds a grant. The `system/` area is read-only in every scope regardless.

Under MCP, every tool call runs all three. Without MCP, the resolver runs once per `bind_tools` call, which is why you [bind per request](integrate-without-mcp.md#per-request). The agent never sees credentials and never passes an entity ID. It passes `scope`, `area`, and `name`, and the tool layer fills in the entity ID from the caller's grant for that scope. A caller cannot name another user's path.

## A complete example

The example is a novelist's assistant served over HTTP to an author (Tianlong), an editor (Diya), and the press's editor-in-chief (Kuixing). Each request carries a bearer token and, optionally, a project header. The server has three scopes:

- `user`: the caller's own ID from the verified token.
- `project`: the manuscript named in `X-Project-Id`, if the caller is a member of it. Tianlong is its `author` and Diya its `editor`. A request with no project header gets no `project` scope, which is what Kuixing's requests look like.
- `organization`: the caller's publisher, Hanlin Press, writable only by admins and owners. Kuixing is an `admin`. Tianlong and Diya are `member`s and can read it but not write it.

```python
import os
from collections.abc import Callable
from dataclasses import dataclass

from google.cloud import storage
from mcp.server.mcpserver import Context

from wenchang.core import MemoryStore
from wenchang.identity import Identity, ResolutionFailure, ScopeGrant
from wenchang.mcp import build_server
from wenchang.prompts import PromptSlots
from wenchang.scope import ScopePolicy
from wenchang.storage.gcs import GcsStorage
from wenchang.transport import InProcessClient


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Claims:
    """What your identity provider says about a verified token."""

    user_id: str
    org_id: str
    org_role: str  # "member" or "admin"


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Credentials:
    """What the request carries. Both fields are untrusted until the resolver checks them."""

    token: str
    project_id: str | None


class MembershipResolver:
    """Turns a request's credentials into the caller's grants. Must not raise."""

    def __init__(
        self,
        verify_token: Callable[[str], Claims | None],
        project_role: Callable[[str, str], str | None],
    ) -> None:
        self._verify_token = verify_token  # your IdP or session store
        self._project_role = project_role  # your membership database

    def resolve(self, credentials: Credentials | None) -> Identity | ResolutionFailure:
        if credentials is None:
            return ResolutionFailure("Missing bearer token.")
        claims = self._verify_token(credentials.token)
        if claims is None:
            return ResolutionFailure("Invalid or expired token.")
        grants = {
            "user": ScopeGrant(claims.user_id, "owner"),
            "organization": ScopeGrant(claims.org_id, claims.org_role),
        }
        if credentials.project_id is not None:
            # The project comes from a header, so check the user belongs to it.
            role = self._project_role(claims.user_id, credentials.project_id)
            if role is None:
                return ResolutionFailure("Not a member of the requested project.")
            grants["project"] = ScopeGrant(credentials.project_id, role)
        return Identity(grants=grants)


def credentials_from_context(ctx: Context) -> Credentials | None:
    headers = ctx.headers or {}
    auth = headers.get("authorization", "")
    if not auth.startswith("Bearer "):
        return None
    return Credentials(token=auth.removeprefix("Bearer "), project_id=headers.get("x-project-id"))


# Stand-ins so the file runs; replace both with calls to your own systems.
TOKENS = {
    "tok-tianlong": Claims("u-tianlong", "o-hanlin-press", "member"),  # author
    "tok-diya": Claims("u-diya", "o-hanlin-press", "member"),  # editor
    "tok-kuixing": Claims("u-kuixing", "o-hanlin-press", "admin"),  # editor-in-chief
}
PROJECT_ROLES = {
    ("u-tianlong", "p-ninth-examination"): "author",
    ("u-diya", "p-ninth-examination"): "editor",
}


def verify_token(token: str) -> Claims | None:
    return TOKENS.get(token)


def project_role(user_id: str, project_id: str) -> str | None:
    return PROJECT_ROLES.get((user_id, project_id))


# Only admins and owners may write the organization scope.
policy = ScopePolicy({"organization": frozenset({"admin", "owner"})})

bucket = storage.Client(project="my-gcp-project").bucket(os.environ["WENCHANG_BUCKET"])

server = build_server(
    slots=PromptSlots(
        purpose=(
            "You have persistent memory of your work helping an author write a novel: reference "
            "it and save to it with these tools whenever you work on a manuscript."
        ),
        scope_guidance=(
            "There are three scopes. `user` is private to the person you are talking with. "
            "`project` is the manuscript, shared by its author, co-author, and editor; any of "
            "them may write it. `organization` is Hanlin Press, shared by every author and editor "
            "there; only editors-in-chief may write it. Writes to `user` and `project` need no "
            "ask. If a new fact contradicts one stored in a shared scope, show the stored fact "
            "and ask which to keep. If no project is open, you have no `project` scope."
        ),
        seed_areas=(
            "- user: preferences, workflows\n"
            "- project: characters, plot, timeline, style\n"
            "- organization: conventions\n\n"
            "Every scope also has a `system/` area."
        ),
    ),
    client=InProcessClient(
        MemoryStore(GcsStorage(bucket), scope_priority=("user", "project", "organization"))
    ),
    resolver=MembershipResolver(verify_token, project_role),
    policy=policy,
    credentials_from_context=credentials_from_context,
    source="inkwell-web",
    product="Inkwell",
)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    server.run("streamable-http", host="0.0.0.0", port=8000)  # behind your TLS proxy
```

Points to notice:

- **The user ID comes from the token, never from a header.** The project does come from a header, so the resolver checks membership before granting it. Treat every header as a request, not a fact.
- **`verify_token` and `project_role` are yours.** They stand for your identity provider or session store and your membership database. The stubs only make the file run.
- **The resolver does not raise.** A bad credential is a `ResolutionFailure`. The detail is shown to the agent, so never put a token or secret in it. If the resolver raises anyway, or `credentials_from_context` raises, the call fails with a permanent "memory unavailable" error that names only the exception type.
- **Under MCP the resolver runs on every tool call.** Cache inside it if verification is expensive, and expire cache entries with the token.
- **Entity IDs are path segments.** They must be non-empty and must not contain `/`, a backslash, or control characters. Use stable IDs. If a user's ID changes, their old files are still under the old ID.

## Behavior to expect

| Situation | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Resolver returns `ResolutionFailure` | Permanent error carrying your detail. No memory for that call. |
| Agent names a scope the caller has no grant for | `InvalidArgumentError` listing the scopes that are available. |
| Tianlong (a `member`) writes `organization` | `RestrictedScopeError`, reason `role_required`, with the permitted roles. |
| Anyone writes `system/` | `RestrictedScopeError`, reason `system_read_only`. |

> **Reads are not restricted by role.** A caller can read every area, including `system/`, of every scope it holds a grant for. `ScopePolicy` gates writes only. If a scope should not be readable by some people, do not grant it to them.

The prompt also has to match the policy. If only admins can write `organization`, say that in `scope_guidance`, or the agent will try and fail. See [Customizing the prompts](prompts.md#scope-guidance).

## Transports

The example serves streamable HTTP, where each request carries its own credentials. On stdio, one process serves one session, so credentials come from the process environment. [Transports](integrate-new-server.md#transports) covers both. To add the tools to a server you already run, with your own auth in front, see [Integrate: an existing mcp 2.x server](integrate-existing-server.md).

## Test your resolver

`pip install "wenchang[testing] @ git+https://github.com/msiebert/wenchang"` adds pytest mixins in `wenchang.testing`. Subclass `ResolverConformance` and supply fixtures for your resolver, a valid and an invalid credential, your policy, the scopes a valid credential should get, and the roles you use. It checks that valid credentials give an `Identity`, invalid ones give a `ResolutionFailure`, results are consistent, roles are known, and writes follow your policy. Details are in the [reference](reference.md#conformance).

---

HTML version: <https://msiebert.github.io/wenchang/identity.html>


<!-- page: storage.md -->

# Storage and operations

How wenchang uses a GCS bucket, what that costs, and how to erase or export one entity's memory. Everything on this page goes through `MemoryStore` over `GcsStorage` (`wenchang.storage.gcs`), unless it says otherwise. The [reference](reference.md#storage) has the `Storage` protocol and the store's signature.

## The bucket

Memory files are objects in one bucket. One `GcsStorage(bucket)` wraps one `google.cloud.storage.Bucket`. [Quickstart](quickstart.md#bucket) creates one with `gcloud`.

wenchang finds credentials through Application Default Credentials: locally `gcloud auth application-default login`, and on Google Cloud the attached service account. Whatever identity the server runs as needs to read, create, overwrite, delete, and list objects in the bucket. `roles/storage.objectUser` on the bucket grants those. Operator jobs that [purge](#erase) need the same permissions.

> **One bucket, many people.** Every user and project writes into the same bucket under their own path prefix. Access control between users is wenchang's scope rules, not bucket permissions. Anyone who can read the bucket directly can read all of it.

Bucket soft delete and object versioning keep deleted bytes recoverable. Set them to match your retention obligations; see [Deleted bytes in GCS](#deleted-bytes).

## Objects and metadata

Each memory file is one object. Its key is the file's path, `{scope}/{entity_id}/{area}/{name}.md` (see [Concepts](concepts.md#paths)). Its body is the file content as UTF-8, with content type `text/markdown; charset=utf-8`. Its version is the object's generation.

The file metadata is GCS custom metadata on the object, under four keys:

| Stored key | Encoding | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `description` | Plain string, one line. | `Lin Qiao, the protagonist` |
| `aliases` | JSON array of strings, in order. | `["Qiao", "Lin"]` |
| `sources` | JSON array of strings, sorted. | `["claude-code", "inkwell-web"]` |
| `last-updated` | ISO 8601 in UTC with a `Z` suffix. | `2026-10-30T14:02:11.402913Z` |

Tool results and the index show the last one as `last_updated`, with an underscore, and `aliases` and `sources` as arrays. Other keys on an object are ignored.

### Writing objects out of band

Reads and listings parse all four keys and require every one. An object written another way, such as `gcloud storage cp` or the GCS console, without them fails with `MetadataFormatError`: reading that file fails, and so do `list_prefix` and `get_memory_index` for every caller whose grants include that entity. The agent sees an `internal` error naming the key.

Write through a `MemoryStore`, as the [seed script](quickstart.md#seed) does, or set all four keys yourself. A store with an index cache does not see out-of-band writes; [invalidate](#invalidate) the entity afterwards.

## Files per entity

An entity is everything under one `{scope}/{entity_id}/` prefix: one user's private memory, or one project's shared memory. `MemoryStore(max_files_per_entity=...)` caps how many files it holds. The default is 500 (`wenchang.core.DEFAULT_MAX_FILES_PER_ENTITY`); `None` disables the cap, and any other value must be positive (`ValueError` otherwise).

```python
store = MemoryStore(storage, max_files_per_entity=200)  # or None for no cap
```

Only creates are checked: a `write_file` with `expected_version=null` outside `system/`. Replacing a file, `append_line`, `replace_fact`, `delete_file`, and reads never are, so an entity at its cap keeps working on the files it has. Files in `system/` and keys that are not well-formed memory paths are not counted. Deleting a file frees a slot.

At the cap, the create fails with a recoverable `FileQuotaExceededError` whose payload carries `limit` (plus `scope`, `area`, and `name`). If a file already exists at that path, the create fails with `VersionConflictError` instead, as it would below the cap. For scope `user`, area `notes`, name `new`, and a limit of 3, the agent sees:

```
Cannot create a new file at scope user, area notes, name new: memory in scope user is at its limit of 3 files (system/ files not counted). Add this content to an existing file instead (append_line, replace_fact, or write_file with that file's version), or merge related files into one and delete the merged ones with delete_file, then retry.
```

followed by the standard recoverable guidance, so the agent consolidates and retries in the same turn without asking the user.

The cap is soft. Counting and writing are not atomic, so concurrent creates in one entity can exceed it by at most the number of creates racing at the boundary. Each checked create counts the entity's keys with `Storage.list_page`, in pages of `max(limit - count, list_page_size)` keys, stopping once it reaches the limit: at most the limit plus the uncounted keys plus one `list_page_size` page, and usually one list call.

## Index cost

`get_memory_index` is what the agent calls at the start of every session. It costs you in two places.

- **The model's context.** The index is capped at `index_max_bytes`, 65536 by default. Each entry is sized as the UTF-8 bytes of its path, its four stored metadata keys and values (in the encodings above), and its version. Entries are added in index order until the next one would pass the cap; the rest are reported under `capped`. The JSON the agent receives adds field names and punctuation on top of that budget, so the payload is somewhat larger than `index_max_bytes`.
- **Storage calls.** Without a cache, every call lists every object under every granted `{scope}/{entity_id}/` prefix, in pages of `list_page_size`, before it caps anything. Listings never read bodies, but the work grows with the number of files in the caller's entities, and the cap does not reduce it. The [file cap](#file-cap) bounds it per entity.

An index cache removes the listing for entities that have not changed.

## The index cache

You can give `MemoryStore` a cache for `get_memory_index`. The cache is optional, and without one nothing changes. With one, the store caches each entity's listing separately, and every write or delete through the store invalidates that entity's entry. Ordering, the size cap, and `capped` are still worked out on each call, so a cached index has the same shape as an uncached one.

wenchang does not ship a cache server. You supply two functions over the cache you already run, such as Redis.

### What you provide

`wenchang.index_cache.IndexCache(get, set, ttl=None, key_prefix="wenchang:index:")` is a frozen configuration object.

- **`get(key) -> str | None`** returns the value last set for `key`, or `None` if it is absent or expired.
- **`set(key, value, ttl) -> None`** stores `value` under `key`, expiring `ttl` (a `timedelta`) from now. `ttl` is `None` for no expiry.
- **`ttl`** is passed unchanged to every `set`. It must be positive if given.
- **`key_prefix`** starts every key the store writes.

Both functions are required: `set` is how the store invalidates, so a read-only cache cannot work. Keys and values are opaque strings. Do not parse them.

Pass it to the store:

```python
store = MemoryStore(storage, index_cache=IndexCache(get=..., set=..., ttl=timedelta(minutes=10)))
```

`store.index_cache` returns the configured cache, or `None`.

### A Redis example

This adapter uses redis-py. It is an illustration, not something wenchang depends on: install the client yourself.

```python
import os
from datetime import timedelta

import redis
from google.cloud import storage

from wenchang.core import MemoryStore
from wenchang.index_cache import IndexCache
from wenchang.storage.gcs import GcsStorage

# decode_responses=True makes get return str, which the cache must return.
r = redis.Redis.from_url(os.environ["REDIS_URL"], decode_responses=True)


def cache_get(key: str) -> str | None:
    return r.get(key)


def cache_set(key: str, value: str, ttl: timedelta | None) -> None:
    if ttl is None:
        r.set(key, value)
    else:
        r.set(key, value, px=max(1, ttl // timedelta(milliseconds=1)))


index_cache = IndexCache(get=cache_get, set=cache_set, ttl=timedelta(minutes=10))

bucket = storage.Client(project="my-gcp-project").bucket(os.environ["WENCHANG_BUCKET"])
store = MemoryStore(
    GcsStorage(bucket),
    scope_priority=("user", "project", "organization"),
    index_cache=index_cache,
)
```

Points to notice:

- **`get` must return `str`.** redis-py returns `bytes` unless the client is created with `decode_responses=True`. If you share a client that does not decode, decode in `get` instead: `value = r.get(key)`, then `return None if value is None else value.decode()`. A `bytes` result is not an error, but the store treats it as a miss and logs a warning on every call, so the cache never helps.
- **`set` maps `ttl` to an expiry.** A finite `ttl` becomes `px` in milliseconds. `None` stores the key with no expiry.
- **One Redis primary is enough.** The cache needs each key's `get` and `set` to be linearizable, which a single primary provides. See [Guarantees and limits](#cache-limits) for replicas.

### In-process cache

`wenchang.index_cache.InMemoryIndexCache` is a thread-safe cache held in one process, for tests and single-process hosts:

```python
from datetime import timedelta

from wenchang.index_cache import IndexCache, InMemoryIndexCache

cache = InMemoryIndexCache()
index_cache = IndexCache(get=cache.get, set=cache.set, ttl=timedelta(minutes=5))
store = MemoryStore(storage, index_cache=index_cache)
```

It drops expired entries only when they are read, so with `ttl=None` it grows without bound. A host that runs several instances needs a shared cache: each instance's in-process cache misses the other instances' writes.

### Writes that bypass the cache

`write_file`, `append_line`, `replace_fact`, and `delete_file` on a store that has the cache invalidate the entity themselves, whether the storage call succeeded or raised. Anything else that changes files in the bucket does not. That includes:

- a seeding job or admin tool,
- another `MemoryStore` built without the cache (such as the [seed script](quickstart.md#seed)),
- a direct write through `gcloud` or the GCS API, including a [restore](#export).

The simplest fix is to give those writers the same `IndexCache`. Otherwise, after they finish, call `MemoryStore.invalidate_index(scope, entity_id)` on a store that has the cache:

```python
seed_store = MemoryStore(GcsStorage(bucket))  # no cache, so its writes do not invalidate
# ... seed_store writes under organization/o-hanlin-press/ ...
cached_store = MemoryStore(GcsStorage(bucket), index_cache=index_cache)
cached_store.invalidate_index("organization", "o-hanlin-press")
```

The next `get_memory_index` that includes that entity lists storage again. `invalidate_index` also overwrites the entity's cached listing, so deleted descriptions and aliases do not stay in your cache. A [purge](#erase) calls it once all of its deletes finish.

`invalidate_index` raises `TypeError` for a non-`str` argument and `ValueError` for an invalid scope or entity ID, before touching the cache. It does nothing on a store with no cache. Unlike the store's own invalidation, it does not swallow cache errors: if `set` raises, so does `invalidate_index`, because the caller asked for the invalidation and should know it did not happen.

A writer that does not invalidate leaves the entity stale until its next write through the cached store, or until `ttl` expires.

### When the cache fails

The cache never makes a memory operation fail.

- If `get` raises, or returns something that is not a `str`, the store logs a warning and lists storage as if nothing were cached.
- If `set` raises, the store logs a warning and skips the store or invalidation. Writes still return their normal result.

Warnings go to the `wenchang.core` logger. They name the scope and the exception or result type, never the entity ID or the key. An exception that is not an `Exception` subclass (such as `KeyboardInterrupt`) still propagates. Storage errors while listing propagate as they do without a cache, and nothing is cached for that entity.

A swallowed invalidation failure leaves the entity's old listing in place, and only `ttl` bounds how long it is served. Watch for these warnings.

### Guarantees and limits

The store keeps a random generation token for each entity. A reader records the token before listing storage and tags its cached listing with it. Every write replaces the token after its storage call, so a listing taken before that write is never served afterwards, even if it is stored late. What this does not cover:

- **`ttl=None` means unbounded staleness.** Tokens cannot detect a write that did not invalidate: an out-of-band write, or an invalidation whose `set` failed. With a finite `ttl`, such an entity is stale for at most `ttl`. With `ttl=None`, it stays stale until something invalidates it or your cache evicts the key. Use a finite `ttl` in production.
- **Timed-out writes.** A write that raised `BackendUnavailableError` (for example a timeout) may still commit in GCS after the store has replaced the token. A reader in between can cache the listing from before the commit under the new token. That listing is served until the entity's next write or invalidation, or until `ttl` expires.
- **Deleted metadata can linger, unserved.** A reader that listed before a delete can store its pre-delete listing after the delete overwrote it. Its tag is stale, so it is never served, but it stays in your cache until the entity is indexed again or `ttl` expires. If you have erasure obligations, a finite `ttl` is required, not just recommended.
- **Per-key linearizable `get` and `set`.** A cache where a `get` can miss an earlier `set` to the same key, such as one reading from asynchronous replicas, bounds freshness only by `ttl`. Operations do not need to be atomic across keys.
- **One `key_prefix` per storage root.** Keys do not identify the bucket. Stores over different buckets or roots that share one cache need distinct prefixes, and no prefix may be a string prefix of another (`"a:"` and `"a:b:"` collide, because scope and entity names may contain `:`). End each prefix in a delimiter and keep them distinct. This is not checked at runtime.
- **Large entities make large values.** A cached listing holds one entry per file in the entity.

> **The cache holds memory metadata.** Cached values contain each file's description, aliases, and sources. Keys contain scope names and entity IDs, which are often user IDs. Your cache inherits the same data-handling obligations as the bucket. File content is never cached.

## Timeouts and retries

wenchang has no timeout or retry setting of its own. `GcsStorage` calls google-cloud-storage with that library's defaults, plus one loop:

- **`get` retries a generation race.** It reads the object's metadata, then downloads the body only if the generation is unchanged. If the object was replaced or deleted in between, it starts over, up to 3 attempts, then raises `BackendUnavailableError`.
- **Timeout.** Each GCS request uses google-cloud-storage's default timeout, 60 seconds.
